overview: This Gujarat is the western Indian sultanate, shown during Mahmud Begada’s reign. Its ports connected prosperous workshops and inland capitals with the Indian Ocean. The imported 1492 to 1500 outline is a short map window, not the dynasty’s lifetime or a map of the modern state.

periods.title: An independent sultanate
periods.summary: Muzaffar Shah formally assumed the title of sultan in 1407; Ahmad Shah developed a new capital.

periods.title: Mahmud Begada’s long reign
periods.summary: Champaner became a new royal capital after Mahmud’s conquest in 1484.

periods.title: Successors and Mughal conquest
periods.summary: Akbar’s campaign reached Gujarat in 1572 and Surat in 1573.

items.text: Ahmad Shah founded Ahmedabad in 1411. Its Islamic monuments drew on the skills of local builders and on regional Hindu and Jain architectural traditions. Pillars, carved screens and open courtyards give the city’s mosques a distinct local character: new royal patrons hired people who already knew how to build beautifully.

After taking the fortified hill of Pavagadh in 1484, Mahmud Begada built a capital at Champaner below it. The resulting landscape combines an older sacred hill, defensive works, palace remains and monumental mosques. A change of ruler did not wipe the ground clean before the next city appeared.

The early sixteenth-century traveler Duarte Barbosa described exports including cotton cloth, silk, dyes, grain and pulses. Horses and pearls came in through overseas trade. Gujarat’s importance rested on busy production and exchange as well as armies: merchants needed useful cargo, not just impressive royal titles.

A cotton fragment made in Gujarat in the fifteenth or sixteenth century was found at Fustat in Egypt. Its printed pattern survives after the cloth itself traveled far from its workshop. This small museum object supplies physical evidence for the overseas reach of Gujarati textiles.

Another cotton fragment, probably from Ahmedabad, used wax to keep parts of the fabric from absorbing indigo dye. Removing the resist revealed the pattern. Flowers and geometric shapes emerged from a carefully planned sequence of covering and coloring, a little like drawing a picture that only appears after its bath.

sections.title: Homes, errands and the work of water

items.text: Excavations at Champaner distinguish spacious compounds with gardens, animal areas and servants’ quarters from modest houses with one to three rooms. Some smaller homes shared protective compound walls. The capital contained different household budgets, not a city full of miniature palaces.

Shops stood along roads and at junctions; many occupied a single room, while larger ones could have underground storage. Archaeologists also recorded gravel road surfaces and stone paving on slopes. Shopping, storing goods and moving animals helped shape the city’s everyday layout.

The capital used a landscape of rainwater catchments, embankments, tanks, channels, wells and cisterns, including older works on the hill. Collecting seasonal rain required people to understand slopes and runoff. A tank’s water supply began well beyond the tank itself.

Some tanks serving mosques and wealthy houses had waterproof plaster and drains placed low enough to empty them for cleaning. Even an elegant water tank needed maintenance. Its practical plumbing mattered alongside the carved architecture around it.

In 1499, Rudabai funded the Adalaj stepwell from her own treasury. Women could be substantial architectural patrons, commissioning structures that joined access to water with elaborate stonework. The surviving work has firmer historical footing than romantic stories later told about its patron.

Bai Harir, a senior woman in the royal household, sponsored another remarkable well near Ahmedabad. Its Sanskrit inscription dates to 1499 and presents water as a benefit for living beings, including people, animals and plants. Public usefulness could be part of a patron’s claim to lasting remembrance.

The stepwell exhibition’s historians describe water collection as women’s work and wells as places for meeting and conversation. Their account spans a long history rather than one recorded day. Descending into a cooler space could bring a social pause into a demanding household chore.

Bai Harir’s well carries the Sanskrit invocation नमामि विश्वकर्माणं, literally “I bow to Vishvakarman.” The words address the divine craftsman. This is a short passage in Nagari script from a real dedicatory inscription, rather than a reconstructed conversation between ordinary residents.

Two illustrated Jain Kalpasutra leaves from Gujarat, dated about 1450, use costly blue pigment and gold. Donating such manuscripts to monastic libraries earned religious merit and supported learning. Beautiful books were valuable possessions that donors deliberately placed in a community’s care.

The Kalpasutra’s wider religious life includes teaching monks and lay followers, recitation and ritual processions during Paryushan. The Walters manuscript account helps explain why a book might be listened to, carried and honored as well as read. These practices belong to the Shvetambara Jain tradition described by the museum.

Modern conservators have used X-rays and infrared imaging to investigate drawings beneath Jain manuscript paintings. One studied leaf comes from Gujarat around the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century. Scientific imaging can uncover stages of an artist’s work without peeling away the finished picture.

Champaner ceased to be the capital and was abandoned as a royal city in 1536. Its later history still included village life and pilgrimage on Pavagadh. Palace ruins record a political departure; they do not mean that every person left the surrounding landscape forever.

A Mughal painting made around 1590 to 1595 celebrates Akbar’s Gujarat campaign and the 1573 victory at Surat. It was produced after the events for an imperial history. Its dramatic scene tells us about how the victors wanted their conquest remembered.

ending.text: Akbar conquered the sultanate in 1572 and 1573. Muzaffar III later renewed resistance, including in 1583, but Gujarat became a Mughal province. Trade and skilled production continued through the political transition. The map’s 1500 endpoint falls decades before that conquest.
